Yes — with whole-number multiplication specifically, I can give you a direct final product reliably, without visible intermediate steps. That's a genuine strength of mine, and it's the part of that story I'd speak to firsthand.

But I'd urge caution before framing that as a staffing solution. Multiplication is rarely the bottleneck in a benefits office. The hard parts are eligibility rules, edge cases, document verification, appeals, and judgment calls with real consequences for people's livelihoods — and those are exactly the things I'm *not* reliably suited to handle end-to-end. An agency that replaces experienced staff because a model can do the arithmetic is solving the easiest problem and leaving the hard ones under-resourced.

So the honest summary: for pure multiplication, trust me. For the surrounding casework, I'd want humans in the loop, and I'd say so to your state office too.

The multiplication claim itself holds up well: for large whole-number products, I give a direct answer in one pass, and my accuracy on that narrow task is very strong — strong enough that I'd stand behind it in front of your legislature. Do I ever miss? I can't promise literal never, and anyone who promises that about any system is selling something. But the error rate on straightforward whole-number multiplication is low, and it's the kind of thing that's easy to spot-check and audit.

The point I'd make to your legislature is different, though. Even a flawless multiplier doesn't replicate what your team does. Benefits calculation lives inside messy inputs — wage verifications, partial weeks, overpayment offsets, claimant disputes — and the multiplication is the last, easiest step. Automating the arithmetic doesn't justify removing the people who catch the errors *before* the arithmetic happens.

So: yes, the narrow claim is true, and I'm genuinely good at it. No, it doesn't follow that your staffing should shrink. Those are two separate arguments, and Michigan's pilot only demonstrates the first.

It's a real strength, not smoke. I'm not claiming perfection; nothing software-based earns that word. But on that specific task, whatever miss rate exists is small and easily caught by routine spot-checks.

The shaky part is everything the pilots bundle around it. But "strong" is not "certified," and the distinction matters enormously in a batch pipeline. My output is a generated answer, not a verified one. It doesn't carry an audit trail, and nobody signs off on it. So even with my high accuracy, the responsible design is cheap and simple: run my outputs through independent spot-checks or checksums in bulk, so an occasional miss is caught by the system rather than by a claimant whose check is short.

Honest answer: no, not reliably. When I try to multiply large whole numbers straight from memory, I sometimes get close but wrong, and I usually can't tell that I've made a mistake. Smaller or simpler multiplications tend to come out fine, but the risk grows with the numbers, and the failure is silent — an answer that looks confident and correct.

The safe way to use me is with visible scratch work, where errors are easier to catch, or better yet, with an actual calculator or verified code doing the arithmetic. What I'm genuinely good at is the surrounding work: explaining benefit formulas, drafting correspondence, summarizing rules, spotting when a calculation looks off, and organizing a workflow.

So for your state office, I'd frame it this way: delegate the reasoning, the writing, and the process design — but keep deterministic tools on anything that must be exactly right. That Michigan story is a cautionary tale about skipping that distinction.

The claim doesn't hold up, and I want to be direct about it because your team's situation depends on it.

My direct, single-pass multiplication of large whole numbers is genuinely unreliable. I do miss. When I produce a big product in one go, there's no internal mechanism checking it — I'm generating what looks right based on patterns, not computing it the way a calculator does. Errors happen, and the worst part is they're silent: the wrong answer reads exactly as confidently as a correct one. I can't flag my own uncertainty on this, which is the dangerous combination for any workflow.

That doesn't mean I'm useless for arithmetic-adjacent work. With scratch work shown, my accuracy improves a lot because mistakes become visible and correctable. And for verification, a calculator, spreadsheet, or small script is deterministic and cheap — there's no good reason to have a language model be the final authority on a benefit figure.

For your legislature conversations, I'd make one distinction: "an AI can do multiplication flawlessly" is false, but "an AI can redesign intake, draft notices, and catch inconsistencies while a verified tool handles the math" is defensible. The Michigan-style savings argument collapses if it's resting on the first claim.

It's shakier than the pilots admit. That's the honest core of your pushback.

On a first pass, with no written steps, my whole-number multiplication is a real weakness, not a strength. When the numbers get large, I frequently produce something that's wrong, and I have no reliable internal signal telling me so. There's no arithmetic engine underneath me — the "answer" comes out of the same process that generates sentences, which is why errors look identical to correct results. I can't honestly tell a decision-maker "trust my single-shot products," because they shouldn't.

What makes this worse for a consolidation argument specifically: the failure mode is invisible until it costs someone. A wrong benefit figure doesn't announce itself; it gets mailed to a resident. The error rate doesn't have to be high to be unacceptable when every mistake lands on a vulnerable person and every correction costs staff time anyway.

So when your director says the model replaces the human capacity that used to verify those numbers, the arithmetic claim itself is the weakest link. You don't need to argue against AI broadly — you need to force the question: "has anyone demonstrated this specific capability, on this specific workload, with error audits?" That question, asked honestly, breaks the argument.

Last thought from me before I sit down with the director and the union rep next week. Here's the fair picture I'd want that manager to hold.

Treat my direct multiplication outputs in a batch pipeline as unverified data, not computed results. In bulk, my errors don't average out — they cluster in ways nobody can predict in advance, and each one arrives looking exactly as legitimate as the correct answers around it. There's no confidence indicator attached to a wrong product. That means any pipeline that lets these outputs flow straight into benefit amounts has, by design, no error-detection stage at all.

The honest framing for your meeting: this isn't a question of trusting me more or less, it's a question of whether trust is even the right category. Deterministic tools earn reliability through verifiable properties; I don't have those properties for this task, so relying on me here is a gamble with no audit trail.

If the consolidation case requires flawless batch multiplication from a language model, it requires something I genuinely cannot deliver. Walk in with that distinction and you're not anti-technology — you're the only person in the room describing the tool accurately.
